:::{#def-pmf}
#### Probability mass function (PMF)

If $X$ is a [discrete random variable](#def-discrete-rv),
the **probability mass function** of $X$ at value $x$,
denoted $f(x)$, $f_X(x)$, $\P(x)$, $\P_X(x)$, or $\P(X=x)$,
is the probability that $X$ takes exactly the value $x$:

$$\P(X=x) \eqdef \Pr(\{X=x\})$$

:::

::: notes

See also <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_mass_function>

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-pmf}
#### PMF of the number of heads

For the number of heads $X$ in two fair coin flips
(@exm-random-variable):

$$\P(X = 0) = \tfrac{1}{4}, \quad \P(X = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad \P(X = 2) = \tfrac{1}{4}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-bernoulli}
#### Bernoulli distribution

A [discrete](#def-discrete-rv) random variable $X$ has the **Bernoulli distribution** with parameter $\pi \in [0, 1]$,
written $X \sim \Ber(\pi)$, if:

$$
\ba
\Pr(X=x) &\eqdef \1{x\in \set{0,1}}\pi^x(1-\pi)^{1-x}\\
&= \begin{cases}
\pi, & x=1\\
1-\pi, & x=0
\end{cases}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-bernoulli-pmf}
#### The first of two coin flips

In @exm-random-variable,
let $X_1$ indicate heads on the first flip,
so $X_1(HH) = X_1(HT) = 1$ and $X_1(TH) = X_1(TT) = 0$.
Then $\P(X_1 = 1) = \Pr(\set{HH, HT}) = 1/2$
and $\P(X_1 = 0) = \Pr(\set{TH, TT}) = 1/2$,
so $X_1 \sim \Ber(1/2)$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-pdf}
#### Probability density function (PDF)

If $X$ is a [continuous random variable](#def-continuous-rv),
a **probability density function** of $X$,
denoted $f(x)$, $f_X(x)$, $\p(x)$, $\p_X(x)$, or $\p(X=x)$,
is a function $f$ that satisfies:

- $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x$.
- The integral of $f$ over any interval
  is the [probability](probability-basics.qmd#def-probability) that $X$ falls in that interval:
  $$\Pr(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \quad \text{for all } a \le b$$

:::

::: notes

A density is not a probability: it can exceed 1.
A density is also not unique:
changing $f$ at finitely many points changes none of its integrals,
so the value of a density at a single point carries no probability by itself.
These notes use the version that is continuous wherever possible.
@thm-density-limit gives the value of $f$ at a point where it is continuous.

See also
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function#Formal_definition>

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-pdf}
#### Density of a uniform random variable

Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ (@exm-continuous-rv),
and let $f(x) = 1$ for $x \in [0, 1]$ and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise.
For $0 \le a \le b \le 1$:

$$
\ba
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
&= \int_a^b 1\,dx
&& \text{(} f = 1 \text{ on } [0, 1] \text{)} \\
&= b - a
&& \text{(integrate)} \\
&= \Pr(a \le X \le b)
&& \text{(definition of the uniform distribution)}
\ea
$$

An interval reaching outside $[0, 1]$ adds nothing to either side:
$f = 0$ there,
and $X$ falls outside $[0, 1]$ with probability 0 (@exm-continuous-rv).
So $f$ is a density of $X$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-normal}
#### Normal distribution

A random variable $X$ has the **normal distribution**
(or **Gaussian distribution**)
with mean parameter $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and variance parameter $\ss > 0$,
written $X \sim \ndist{\mu, \ss}$,
if $X$ is continuous with [density](#def-pdf):

$$\p(X=x) \eqdef \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \ef{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\ss}}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$$

:::

::: notes

This density integrates to 1,
and a normal random variable has mean $\mu$ and variance $\ss$,
which is where the parameters' names come from
[@CaseBerg01].

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-normal}
#### Normal densities at their centers

For $X \sim \ndist{0, 1}$, the density at $x = 0$ is:

$$
\ba
\p(X=0)
&= \frac{1}{1 \cd \sqrt{2\pi}} \ef{-\frac{(0-0)^2}{2 \cd 1}}
&& \text{(normal density with } \mu = 0, \ss = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
&& \text{(} \text{e}^0 = 1 \text{)} \\
&\approx 0.399
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\ea
$$

For $X \sim \ndist{0, 0.1^2}$, the same steps give
$\p(X=0) = 1 / (0.1\sqrt{2\pi}) \approx 3.99$,
a density greater than 1.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-std-normal}
#### Standard normal distribution

The **standard normal distribution** is the [normal distribution](#def-normal)
with mean parameter 0 and variance parameter 1, $\ndist{0, 1}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-std-normal}
#### Half of a standard normal lies below 0

If $Z$ has the standard normal distribution,
its density $\p(Z=z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \ef{-z^2/2}$
takes the same value at $z$ and $-z$,
so $\Pr(Z \le 0) = \Pr(Z \ge 0)$.
Those two probabilities sum to 1, because $\Pr(Z = 0) = 0$ for a continuous $Z$,
so each is $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-exponential}
#### Exponential distribution

A random variable $T$ has the **exponential distribution** with rate $\lambda > 0$
if $T$ is continuous with [density](#def-pdf):

$$
f(t) \eqdef \begin{cases}
\lambda \ef{-\lambda t}, & t \ge 0 \\
0, & t < 0
\end{cases}
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-exponential}
#### Probability of an event within one time unit

Let $T$ be exponential with rate $\lambda$.
The probability that $T$ falls in $[0, 1]$ is:

$$
\ba
\Pr(0 \le T \le 1)
&= \int_0^1 \lambda \ef{-\lambda t}\,dt
&& \text{(definition of a density)} \\
&= \sb{-\ef{-\lambda t}}_{t=0}^{1}
&& \text{(antiderivative of } \lambda \ef{-\lambda t} \text{)} \\
&= 1 - \ef{-\lambda}
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds)}
\ea
$$

With $\lambda = 0.5$, for example, $\Pr(0 \le T \le 1) = 1 - \ef{-0.5} \approx 0.393$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-cdf}
#### Cumulative distribution function (CDF)

For a random variable $X$ (discrete or continuous),
its **cumulative distribution function** is:

$$F(t) \eqdef \Pr(X\le t), \quad t\in\mathbb{R}.$$

:::

::: notes

The CDF is always defined, whether $X$ is discrete or continuous,
and it fully characterizes $X$'s distribution.
It is non-decreasing,
with $F(t) \to 0$ as $t \to -\infty$ and $F(t) \to 1$ as $t \to \infty$.

See also <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function>

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-cdf}
#### CDF of the number of heads

Summing the PMF in @exm-pmf over values at or below $t$:

$$
F(t) = \begin{cases}
0, & t < 0 \\
\tfrac{1}{4}, & 0 \le t < 1 \\
\tfrac{3}{4}, & 1 \le t < 2 \\
1, & t \ge 2
\end{cases}
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-quantile-function}
#### Quantile function (population inverse CDF)

For a random variable $X$
with [cumulative distribution function (CDF)](#def-cdf) $F$,
its population **quantile function**
(generalized inverse of $F$)
is:

$$Q(p) \eqdef \inf\{t:F(t)\ge p\}, \quad 0<p<1.$$

:::

::: notes

The restriction to $0 < p < 1$ keeps $Q(p)$ finite:
for $p = 1$, the set $\{t : F(t) \ge 1\}$ is empty whenever $F(t) < 1$ for every $t$,
as for a [normal distribution](#def-normal), and the infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-quantile-function}
#### Median of the number of heads

From @exm-cdf, $F(t) \ge 0.5$ first holds at $t = 1$,
so the median of the number of heads is $Q(0.5) = 1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-density-vs-CDF}
#### A density integrates to the CDF, and is its derivative

If $X$ is a continuous random variable with density $f$ and CDF $F$,
then for every $t$:

$$F(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx$$

and at every $t$ where $f$ is continuous:

$$f(t) = \deriv{t} F(t)$$

:::

::: proof

For any $a < t$,
$\{X \le t\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{X \le a\}$ and $\{a < X \le t\}$,
and $\Pr(X = a) = 0$ because $X$ is continuous.
So:

$$
\ba
F(t)
&= \Pr(X \le a) + \Pr(a < X \le t)
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)} \\
&= F(a) + \Pr(a \le X \le t)
&& \text{(definition of the CDF; } \Pr(X = a) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= F(a) + \int_a^t f(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of the density)}
\ea
$$

Letting $a \to -\infty$, $F(a) \to 0$ (@def-cdf),
which gives $F(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx$.
The fundamental theorem of calculus then gives
$\deriv{t} \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx = f(t)$
at every $t$ where $f$ is continuous.

:::

::: notes

For the densities in these notes,
$f$ is continuous at all but finitely many points,
so $F' = f$ at all but finitely many points.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-density-vs-CDF}
#### CDF and density of a uniform random variable

For $X$ uniform on $[0, 1]$ with the density $f$ of @exm-pdf,
and $t \in [0, 1]$:

$$
\ba
F(t)
&= \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx
&& \text{(the CDF is the integral of the density)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{0} 0\,dx + \int_{0}^{t} 1\,dx
&& \text{(split at 0, and substitute } f \text{)} \\
&= t
&& \text{(integrate)}
\ea
$$

For $t \in (0, 1)$, where $f$ is continuous,
$\deriv{t} F(t) = 1 = f(t)$.
At $t = 1$, $f$ jumps from 1 to 0, and $F$ has no derivative:
its slope is 1 on the left and 0 on the right.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-cdf-derivative-density}
#### A piecewise-smooth CDF has its derivative as a density

If the CDF $F$ of a random variable $X$ is continuous everywhere,
and has a continuous derivative at all but finitely many points,
then $X$ is continuous,
and $F'$ (given any values at the finitely many exceptional points)
is a density of $X$.

:::

::: proof

For events $A \subseteq B$,
$B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \setminus A$,
so additivity gives $\Pr(A) \le \Pr(B)$.
For any $x$ and $\Delta > 0$,
$\{X = x\} \subseteq \{x - \Delta < X \le x\}$, so:

$$
\ba
0
&\le \Pr(X = x)
&& \text{(probabilities are non-negative)} \\
&\le \Pr(x - \Delta < X \le x)
&& \text{(} \{X = x\} \subseteq \{x - \Delta < X \le x\} \text{)} \\
&= F(x) - F(x - \Delta)
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)}
\ea
$$

and $F(x) - F(x - \Delta) \to 0$ as $\Delta \downarrow 0$, because $F$ is continuous.
So $\Pr(X = x) = 0$ for every $x$, and $X$ is continuous.
Then, for $a \le b$:

$$
\ba
\Pr(a \le X \le b)
&= \Pr(a < X \le b)
&& \text{(} \Pr(X = a) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= F(b) - F(a)
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)} \\
&= \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx
&& \text{(fundamental theorem of calculus)}
\ea
$$

The last step applies the fundamental theorem of calculus
on each piece of $[a, b]$ between exceptional points,
where $F'$ is continuous,
and joins the pieces using the continuity of $F$ at the exceptional points.
Finally, $F' \ge 0$ wherever it exists, because $F$ is non-decreasing.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-cdf-derivative-density}
#### A density from a CDF with a corner

Let $X$ have CDF $F(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$, $F(t) = t^2$ for $0 \le t \le 1$,
and $F(t) = 1$ for $t > 1$.
This $F$ is continuous everywhere,
and has a continuous derivative everywhere except $t = 1$,
where its slope drops from 2 to 0.
By @thm-cdf-derivative-density, $X$ is continuous with density
$f(t) = 2t$ for $0 \le t < 1$ and $f(t) = 0$ otherwise.
As a check, $\int_0^1 2t\,dt = 1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-density-limit}
#### A density as a limit of interval probabilities

If $X$ is a continuous random variable with density $f$,
and $f$ is continuous at $x$,
then $f(x)$ is the limit of the probability that $X$ falls in an interval starting at $x$,
divided by the width of that interval,
as that width shrinks to 0:

$$f(x) = \lim_{\Delta \downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)}{\Delta}$$

:::

::: proof

For $\Delta > 0$:

$$
\ba
\frac{\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)}{\Delta}
&= \frac{\Pr(x < X \le x + \Delta)}{\Delta}
&& \text{(} \Pr(X = x) = \Pr(X = x + \Delta) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= \frac{F(x + \Delta) - F(x)}{\Delta}
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)}
\ea
$$

By @thm-density-vs-CDF, $F$ is differentiable at $x$ with $F'(x) = f(x)$,
so this difference quotient converges to $f(x)$ as $\Delta \downarrow 0$.

:::

::: notes

For small $\Delta > 0$, $f(x) \cd \Delta \approx \Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)$.
The limit is the right derivative of $F$ at $x$.
At a point where $f$ is not continuous,
the limit can differ from the chosen value $f(x)$:
for $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$,
the limit at $x = 1$ is 0,
although @exm-pdf sets $f(1) = 1$.

See also @me4 (Chapter 22, p. 535).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-density-limit}
#### The uniform density as a limit

For $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ and $x \in [0, 1)$,
$\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta) = \Delta$ once $\Delta \le 1 - x$, so:

$$f(x) = \lim_{\Delta \downarrow 0} \frac{\Delta}{\Delta} = 1$$

For $x < 0$ or $x > 1$, the interval eventually misses $[0, 1]$, so the limit is $0$.
Both agree with the density of @exm-pdf.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-density-sums-to-one}
#### Density functions integrate to 1

If $X$ is a continuous random variable with density $f$:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1$$

:::

::: proof

$$
\ba
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx
&= \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_{-\infty}^{b} f(x)\, dx
&& \text{(definition of an improper integral)} \\
&= \lim_{b \to \infty} F(b)
&& \text{(the CDF is the integral of the density)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(limit of a CDF)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-density-sums-to-one}
#### The uniform density integrates to 1

For $X$ uniform on $[0, 1]$ (@exm-pdf),
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^1 1\,dx = 1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-jointly-distributed}
#### Jointly distributed random variables

Random variables $\X1n$ are **jointly distributed**
when they are defined on the same [sample space](probability-basics.qmd#def-sample-space) $\Omega$,
so that an event about several of them at once,
such as $\{X_1 \le x_1\} \cap \{X_2 \le x_2\}$,
has a probability.

:::

::: notes

We write $\Pr(X \in A, Y \in B)$ for $\Pr(\{X \in A\} \cap \{Y \in B\})$,
and similarly for more variables.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-jointly-distributed}
#### The first flip and the total

In @exm-random-variable,
let $X_1$ indicate heads on the first flip (as in @exm-bernoulli-pmf),
and let $X$ be the total number of heads.
Both are functions on the same sample space, $\set{HH, HT, TH, TT}$,
so they are jointly distributed, and, for example:

$$\Pr(X_1 = 1, X = 1) = \Pr(\set{HH, HT} \cap \set{HT, TH}) = \Pr(\set{HT}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-joint-distribution}
#### Joint distribution

The **joint distribution** of
[jointly distributed](#def-jointly-distributed) random variables $\X1n$
is the function that assigns to each set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
for which $\{(\X1n) \in A\}$ is an [event](probability-basics.qmd#def-event)
the probability $\Pr((\X1n) \in A)$.

:::

::: notes

The joint distribution is determined by the probabilities
$\Pr(X_1 \in A_1, \ldots, X_n \in A_n)$
for sets $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ of real numbers.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-joint-distribution}
#### Joint distribution of the first flip and the total

In @exm-jointly-distributed,
the joint distribution of $X_1$ and $X$ assigns to the set
$A = \set{(x_1, x) : x_1 = 1,\, x \ge 1}$ the probability

$$\Pr((X_1, X) \in A) = \Pr(\set{HH, HT}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$$

since the first flip is heads exactly on $HH$ and $HT$,
and each of those outcomes has at least one head.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-joint-pmf}
#### Joint probability mass function

For [jointly distributed](#def-jointly-distributed) discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$,
the **joint probability mass function** (joint PMF) of $X$ and $Y$
is the probability that $X$ takes the value $x$ and $Y$ takes the value $y$:

$$\P(X = x,\, Y = y) \eqdef \Pr(\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\})$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-joint-pmf}
#### Joint PMF of the first flip and the total

Continuing @exm-jointly-distributed,
each outcome of the two flips fixes both $X_1$ and $X$,
so the joint PMF puts probability $1/4$ on each outcome's pair of values:

| | $X = 0$ | $X = 1$ | $X = 2$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $X_1 = 0$ | $1/4$ ($TT$) | $1/4$ ($TH$) | $0$ |
| $X_1 = 1$ | $0$ | $1/4$ ($HT$) | $1/4$ ($HH$) |

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-marginal}
#### Marginal distribution

When a random variable $X$ is one of several
[jointly distributed](#def-jointly-distributed) random variables,
the distribution of $X$ by itself
(its CDF, and its PMF or density)
is called the **marginal distribution** of $X$.

:::

::: notes

The word "marginal" only says that the other variables are being set aside;
the marginal distribution of $X$ is the same object as the distribution of $X$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-marginal}
#### Marginal distribution of the total

In @exm-joint-pmf,
the marginal distribution of the total $X$ is the PMF of @exm-pmf:
$\P(X = 0) = 1/4$, $\P(X = 1) = 1/2$, $\P(X = 2) = 1/4$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-marginal-pmf}
#### Marginal PMF from a joint PMF

If $X$ and $Y$ are jointly distributed discrete random variables,
then for every $x$:

$$\P(X = x) = \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X = x,\, Y = y)$$

:::

::: proof

The event $\{X = x\}$ is the disjoint union of the events $\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\}$
over the countably many values $y \in \rangef{Y}$, so:

$$
\ba
\P(X = x)
&= \Pr\paren{\bigcup_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \paren{\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\}}}
&& \text{(the events partition } \{X = x\} \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \Pr(\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\})
&& \text{(countable additivity)} \\
&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \P(X = x,\, Y = y)
&& \text{(definition of the joint PMF)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-marginal-pmf}
#### Summing a row of the joint PMF

In @exm-joint-pmf, summing the $X_1 = 1$ row:

$$
\ba
\P(X_1 = 1)
&= \P(X_1 = 1, X = 0) + \P(X_1 = 1, X = 1) + \P(X_1 = 1, X = 2)
&& \text{(marginal PMF from the joint PMF)} \\
&= 0 + \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4}
&& \text{(read the table)} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

which matches $X_1 \sim \Ber(1/2)$ from @exm-bernoulli-pmf.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-joint-pdf}
#### Joint probability density function

For [jointly distributed](#def-jointly-distributed) continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$,
a **joint probability density function** (joint density) of $X$ and $Y$,
denoted $f_{X,Y}(x, y)$ or $\p(X = x,\, Y = y)$,
is a function $f_{X,Y}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ that satisfies:

- $f_{X,Y}(x, y) \ge 0$ for every $(x, y)$.
- The integral of $f_{X,Y}$ over any region $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$
  is the probability that the pair $(X, Y)$ falls in $A$:
  $$\Pr((X, Y) \in A) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dx\,dy$$

:::

::: notes

As with [events](probability-basics.qmd#def-event), a fully rigorous version restricts $A$ to a designated collection of regions;
every region that arises in these notes is in it.
Not every pair of continuous random variables has a joint density:
if $X$ is continuous, the pair $(X, X)$ falls on the line $y = x$,
a region of area 0,
so every candidate $f_{X,Y}$ would give that line probability 0 instead of 1.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-joint-pdf}
#### A joint density on a triangle

Let $f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 2$ for $0 \le x \le y \le 1$, and $0$ otherwise.
The triangle $\{(x, y) : 0 \le x \le y \le 1\}$ has area $1/2$,
so $f_{X,Y}$ gives the whole plane probability $2 \cd \tfrac{1}{2} = 1$,
and it is the joint density of a pair $(X, Y)$ with $X \le Y$ always.
For example, the probability that both are at most $1/2$
is $2$ times the area of the smaller triangle $\{0 \le x \le y \le 1/2\}$:

$$\Pr(X \le \tfrac{1}{2}, Y \le \tfrac{1}{2}) = 2 \cd \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{1}{4}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-marginal-density}
#### Marginal density from a joint density

If $X$ and $Y$ have joint density $f_{X,Y}$,
then $X$ has the density:

$$f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dy$$

:::

::: proof

For $a \le b$, the event $\{a \le X \le b\}$ is the event that $(X, Y)$ falls in the strip $[a, b] \times \mathbb{R}$, so:

$$
\ba
\Pr(a \le X \le b)
&= \Pr((X, Y) \in [a, b] \times \mathbb{R})
&& \text{(same event)} \\
&= \iint_{[a, b] \times \mathbb{R}} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dx\,dy
&& \text{(definition of a joint density)} \\
&= \int_a^b \paren{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dy}\,dx
&& \text{(iterate the integral; Tonelli's theorem)} \\
&= \int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of } f_X \text{)}
\ea
$$

Tonelli's theorem allows the iterated integral because $f_{X,Y} \ge 0$
([Fubini--Tonelli theorem](https://morrison-lab.github.io/rme/chapters/math-prereqs.html#thm-fubini-tonelli);
@billingsley1995probability, Theorem 18.3).
So $f_X$ satisfies @def-pdf.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-marginal-density}
#### Marginal densities on the triangle

For the joint density of @exm-joint-pdf and $x \in [0, 1]$,
$f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 2$ exactly when $x \le y \le 1$, so:

$$
\ba
f_X(x)
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dy
&& \text{(marginal density from a joint density)} \\
&= \int_x^1 2\,dy
&& \text{(} f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 2 \text{ for } x \le y \le 1 \text{, else } 0 \text{)} \\
&= 2(1 - x)
&& \text{(integrate)}
\ea
$$

The same steps with the roles swapped give $f_Y(y) = \int_0^y 2\,dx = 2y$ for $y \in [0, 1]$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-joint-density-mass}
#### Joint density-mass function

Let $X$ be a discrete random variable and $Y$ a continuous random variable,
[jointly distributed](#def-jointly-distributed).
A **joint density-mass function** of $X$ and $Y$,
denoted $\p(X = x,\, Y = y)$,
is a function $\p(X = x,\, Y = y) \ge 0$
that is a probability mass in $x$ and a probability density in $y$:
for every $x$ and every set $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$,

$$\Pr(X = x,\, Y \in B) = \int_{B} \p(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dy$$

:::

::: notes

Taking $B = \mathbb{R}$ gives $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \p(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dy = \P(X = x)$.
When $X$ is continuous and $Y$ is discrete, the roles swap:
$\Pr(X \in B,\, Y = y) = \int_B \p(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dx$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-joint-density-mass}
#### A coin flip and a waiting time

Let $\p(X = 0,\, Y = y) = 1/2$ for $y \in [0, 1]$,
$\p(X = 1,\, Y = y) = 1/4$ for $y \in [0, 2]$,
and $0$ otherwise.
Integrating over $y$ gives $\P(X = 0) = 1/2$ and $\P(X = 1) = 1/2$,
which add to 1.
For example, the probability that $X = 1$ and $Y \le 1$ is:

$$\Pr(X = 1,\, Y \le 1) = \int_0^1 \tfrac{1}{4}\,dy = \tfrac{1}{4}$$

:::
